ta-l1d27q1-d1e97.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 27. Having set out the three personal properties, Lombard compares them with the names of the persons. He shows that the properties are designated in the usual personal names (Father, Son, Holy Spirit), since the properties determine the persons and are understood in their names as the determining in the determined, though the mode of signifying differs ('to be Father' and 'to have begotten the Son' are not wholly the same). He shows they are designated in other names signifying the persons too, and then gives a general rule for finding personal names, with a question whether 'God from God, light from light' are said by substance and a conclusion that 'this from this' is said only with names of substance. Thomas asks first about the notions or properties, then about personal names, especially 'Word'. On the first, two articles: how the properties differ from one another, and whether properties or relations conceptually precede the personal operations or conversely.
claims: The properties are designated in the personal names as the determining in the determined.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e134.summary: First argument that the properties are not distinguished from one another. There is no distinction in God except by origin, and one property does not originate from another, as the essence does not beget.
claims: Distinction in God is only by origin.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e137.summary: Second argument. A relation is a medium between two extremes, and between two terms there is one road in reality, though conceptually different, as Thebes to Athens and back (the Philosopher), so one relation relates Father to Son and Son to Father, and paternity and filiation are one relation.
claims: One road between two terms.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e140.summary: Third argument. Nothing is really distinct in God except by relative opposition. As essential attributes like goodness and wisdom are not opposed and are predicated of each other, so the properties of one person are not opposed, or they could not be in one supposit, so they are not several in reality and can be predicated of each other ('paternity is innascibility').
claims: Unopposed properties are one and mutually predicable.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e144.summary: Fourth argument. The concept of Word differs from that of Son no more than the concept of unbegotten from that of Father, and the same notion is designated by 'Word' and 'Son' (as the text says), so innascibility and paternity are one notion.
claims: Word and Son designate one notion.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e147.summary: Fifth argument. One person has only one relation to another, and 'Father', 'generation', and 'paternity' each imply the Father's relation to the Son, so they are all the same, against Lombard.
claims: One relation per pair of persons.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e150.summary: Thomas's determination. In God there are five notions (Dist. 26) but not five things, only three: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Things are properly multiplied, and not one, in that by whose proper differences they are distinguished (the Philosopher): isosceles and equilateral are distinguished by differences of triangle and so are several triangles, but fall under one difference of figure, having three sides, and so are one figure. So only things distinguished by a difference of thing can be called several things, and in God difference of thing is only by relative opposition, so they are several things only as that opposition requires. Paternity and filiation are two things, as are Father and Son, but paternity and common spiration are not two things, since they are not relatively opposed; they are only two relations, distinguished by differences of relation as relation. Since relation is said by respect to another, its differences follow its different terms, and since the Father is related to the Son by paternity and to the Spirit by common spiration, these are two relations and two notions, as different ways of making the Father known.
claims: There are five notions but only three things in God.
Only relatively opposed properties are distinct things; unopposed relations of one person differ as relations by their different terms.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e153.summary: Reply to the first argument. Opposition by origin is conceptually prior in the relations of origin than in the persons who originate from one another, since the persons are opposed only by having these relations. So the opposed relations are distinguished by themselves, like constitutive differences, and the persons by relations, as species by differences.
claims: Opposed relations distinguish themselves; persons are distinguished by relations, as species by differences.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e156.summary: Reply to the second argument. Some held, as Avicenna reports, that the numerically same relation is in both extremes, which cannot be, since one accident is not in two subjects. Rather in each extreme there is a relation differing from the other, in some cases in species, when the extremes have different names (paternity and filiation), in others only numerically, when they share a name (likeness, equality); the relation in one as in its subject is in the other as its term, and conversely. So by its being, as founded in reality, a relation is not a medium but an extreme, though by its respect it is a medium, so paternity and filiation are really distinct.
claims: Each extreme has its own relation; by being a relation is an extreme, by respect a medium.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e159.summary: Reply to the third argument. As the essential attributes are not several things, neither are the properties of one person; they are one thing, the person. But since relation remains in God even by the common character of its genus, the distinction of relations as relations remains, so there are several relations and one is not predicated of another. This is not so for essential attributes, which do not remain in God by a common generic character, so they are not distinguished by a real common character (signified by a first-imposition name), though they share a common character of reason (signified by a second-imposition name), all being attributes; dividing that, they are not predicated of each other as attributes ('this attribute is not that attribute'). But since they do not divide a real common, by divine simplicity they are predicated of each other under any first-imposition name ('this thing is that thing', 'wisdom is goodness').
claims: Properties of one person are one thing but several relations, not mutually predicable.
Essential attributes, not dividing a real common genus, are mutually predicable as things.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e163.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. 'Word' and 'Son' are not distinguished by difference of relation, since both say a relation of the same to the same, so they imply one relation, not two, and likewise 'Gift' and 'Love'. They are distinguished only by their foundations, Son in the emanation of nature and Word in the emanation of intellect, which in God differ only conceptually, so Word and Son differ only conceptually and not by relation. 'Unbegotten' and 'Father' are not said with respect to the same, so they are not one relation or notion.
claims: Word and Son are one relation differing only by conceptual foundation; unbegotten and Father are different notions.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e166.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. As in essentials the divine operation, God, and deity are really the same and distinguished only by a concept grounded in reality, so in personals the personal operation, the person, and the constituting property are really the same and differ only conceptually and in mode of signifying. 'Father', 'paternity', and 'generation' signify the same character, as hypostasis or person, as property, and as operation.
claims: Pater, paternitas, and generatio signify one character by different modes: person, property, operation.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e178.summary: First argument that the personal operation conceptually precedes the relation. Generation signifies a personal operation (Dist. 5), and Lombard says he is Father because he begot.
claims: He is Father because he begot.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e181.summary: Second argument. Paternity and generation follow one another, so either paternity is the principle of generation or follows it as an effect. It is not the principle, since Anselm says he begets by being God, not by being Father.
claims: Anselm: he begets as God, not as Father.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e184.summary: Third argument. Every relation conceptually follows its foundation, as equality follows quantity, and paternity and filiation are founded on operation (the Philosopher).
claims: Relations follow their foundations.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e188.summary: Fourth argument. Active generation relates to the Father as passive generation or birth to the Son, and filiation never precedes birth conceptually, so neither does paternity precede active generation.
claims: Filiation follows birth.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e191.summary: Sed contra. Operation belongs to distinct individuals (the Philosopher), and nothing is distinct in God except by relation, so relation precedes personal operation conceptually.
claims: Operation presupposes distinct individuals.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e194.summary: Second sed contra. The principle of something's proper operation must be its proper form, and generation is the Father's proper operation, and the only form proper to the Father is paternity, so paternity is the principle of generation and precedes it.
claims: Paternity is the proper form and principle of generation.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e197.summary: Thomas's determination. For those who say relations do not distinguish or constitute persons but only manifest them, relation simply follows personal operation conceptually. But since nothing distinguishes and constitutes the persons except relation by its opposition, relation, as constituting the person, conceptually precedes the operation. So relation can be considered three ways: as relation simply, and so it does not precede but rather follows the operation; as divine relation constituting the person and being the subsistent person, and so it precedes the operation; and as the personal operation itself, and so they are conceptually simultaneous and the same.
claims: As constituting the person, relation conceptually precedes the personal operation.
As relation simply it follows; as identical with the operation it is simultaneous.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e200.summary: Reply to the first argument. When Lombard says he is Father because he begot, he takes generation not as operation but as the property constituting the person, and so it precedes the constituted person, as in the previous distinction generation is put for paternity. Or he regards relation as relation, not as divine relation constituting and distinguishing the person. Or, better, 'he is Father because he begot' implies no causal order but identity of relation, since Lombard also says, from Augustine, he is Son because begotten and begotten because Son.
claims: 'Because he begot' expresses identity of relation, not causal order.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e203.summary: Reply to the second argument. As said in Dist. 7, the principle of generation in God is neither the nature alone nor the property alone, but the divine nature as in the Father, or the property that is paternity. So Anselm does not state everything required for the principle of generation; to say it all, he begets not only because he is God, nor only because he is Father, but because he is God the Father.
claims: The principle of generation is the divine nature as in the Father.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e207.summary: Reply to the third argument. The argument holds of relation as relation, but paternity has something more: being divine, it constitutes the person and is the constituted person, and by this it conceptually precedes the operation.
claims: Paternity as divine relation precedes generation.

ta-l1d27q1-d1e210.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Father and Son are not alike here: the proper form of what is begotten is in no way the principle of generation, active or passive, but follows it as a kind of term, so filiation does not precede birth, but the proper form of the begetter is the principle of active generation, so it must precede it.
claims: The begetter's form precedes generation as principle; the begotten's form follows as term.

ta-l1d27q1-Dd1e92.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 27 divides Lombard's comparison of the personal properties with the personal names and his general rule for finding such names. It announces two articles on the properties: how they differ from one another, and whether relations precede the personal operations conceptually.
claims: The properties are designated in the personal names.

ta-l1d27q1-Dd1e126.summary: Article 1 holds that the five notions are not five things but three, since only relatively opposed properties are distinct things. Paternity and common spiration are two relations and notions, differing by their terms, but one thing. Opposed relations distinguish themselves like constitutive differences. Each extreme of a relation has its own relation, so paternity and filiation are really distinct. Unopposed relations of one person are not mutually predicable as relations, unlike essential attributes. Word and Son are one relation differing only by conceptual foundation, while 'unbegotten' and 'Father' are different notions. Father, paternity, and generation signify one character as person, property, and operation.
claims: Five notions, three things: only opposed relations are distinct things.
Father, paternity, and generation differ only in mode of signifying.

ta-l1d27q1-Dd1e170.summary: Article 2 holds that relation, as divine relation constituting the subsistent person, conceptually precedes the personal operation, though as relation simply it follows it and as identical with the operation it is simultaneous. 'He is Father because he begot' expresses identity rather than causal order. The principle of generation is the divine nature as in the Father, and the begetter's form precedes generation as principle while the begotten's follows as term.
claims: Constitutive relation conceptually precedes personal operation.
The principle of generation is God the Father, the nature as in the Father.

ta-l1d27q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 27 treats the notions or properties. Article 1 holds that the five notions are only three things, since only relatively opposed relations are really distinct, and that unopposed relations of one person, like paternity and common spiration, differ as relations by their terms. Word and Son are one relation, 'unbegotten' and 'Father' different notions, and Father, paternity, and generation differ only in mode of signifying. Article 2 holds that relation, as constituting the person, conceptually precedes the personal operation, though considered simply as relation it follows it.
claims: Five notions are three things, distinguished by relative opposition.
Constitutive relation conceptually precedes personal operation.
